newsitem.title: DENMARK: SAS nine-month profits sharply down.
newsitem.headline: SAS nine-month profits sharply down.

text.p: Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS) on Tuesday reported nine-month pre-tax profits sharply down and said it had set in motion widespread cost-cutting plans, but did not detail the reductions.
It logged profit of 1.257 billion Swedish crowns ($190.3 million), compared to 2.145 billion during the first nine months of 1995.

It said that its operating result fell by 753 million crowns in the third quarter, to 259 million crowns and blamed exchange rate fluctuations, higher fuel prices and the cost of improvements to service and quality.

"Wide-ranging action has been set in motion with a view to goal-oriented and structured cost reductions, together with increased revenues, to show effect in 1997 and subsequent years," it said in a statement giving the results.
Cuts have been widely expected as an urgent necessity to restore flagging profitability.
Analysts said this week that savings of one billion Swedish crowns over two years cited in uncomfirmed media reports would not be enough.
"It will come too late and it will too difficult to implement," one said.
The report said that passenger traffic was up five percent over the nine months compared to the same period last year.
It gave no figures for freight.
Net debt was well down, to 1.975 billion Swedish crowns at September 30 1996 from 2.554 billion at December 31 1995 and 4.210 billion at September 30 1995.
The report saw fourth quarter 1996 pre-tax profit on a par with October-December 1995's 487 million Swedish crowns.
It acknowledged that competition had increased and cited Brussels-based Virgin Express as among new European operators.

Virgin Express, a unit of British entrepeneur Richard Branson's Virgin group has introduced twice daily budget flights between Copenhagen and the Belgian capital, triggering a price war which it says it is confident it can win.
Aviation insiders say that British Airways appears to be positioning itself for a major assault on SAS through its franchise agreement with Denmark's Sun-Air.

The new operation, under the name British Airways Express, has already challenged SAS' domination of domestic routes and introduced links from Denmark's second city of Aarhus to the Norwegian and Swedish capitals.
Tuesday's result came too late to effect SAS share prices, but analysts said that the absence of cost-cutting details was likely to disappoint investors.
